 Follow After an Election Day trouncing, Pennsylvania Republicans look to the future
 Peter Hall Mon, November 16, 2026 at 10:11 AM UTC 9 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Poll workers wait for voters at a polling place in a garage on Willett Road in Brentwood, Pennsylvania, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by John Beale/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
 On Election Day, Pennsylvania Republicans suffered their most stunning defeat at the ballot box in at least 50 years, amid turmoil in Washington, another Middle East war and crippling price hikes at home.
 Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro sailed to a second term, while state Democrats expanded their one-seat majority in the state House to 13 and flipped the Senate, which has been under GOP control almost continuously since 1978.
 And four Republican incumbents lost their U.S. House seats, contributing to a nationwide blowout in Congress where Democrats picked up at least 40 seats in the lower chamber and eight in the Senate.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The Capital-Star spoke to Pennsylvania Republicans about what the party can learn from its Election Day rout to prepare for upcoming elections. They include two seats on the state Supreme Court next year, and the U.S. Senate seat held by Democratic Sen. John Fetterman, who is widely expected to face primary challengers in 2028. U.S. Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-4th District) told Politico she is "considering" a run for Senate against Fetterman.
 "Every couple years, the voters have a chance to basically tell you how they're feeling, and they spoke loud and clear that they're unhappy with Republicans," House Minority Leader Jesse Topper (R-Bedford) said. "And I think there are Republicans who are unhappy because they feel we didn't do what we said we were going to do, particularly at a national level."
 House Republican Leader Jesse Topper (R-Bedford) speaks during swearing-in day on the chamber floor on Tuesday, Jan. 7, 2025. (Capital-Star/Peter Hall)
 In that respect, said former Congressman Charlie Dent, the Nov. 3 election was like most midterm elections.
 "This election was a referendum on the president of the United States," Dent said, adding that the backlash this year was notably severe because of what he called "the six Cs": cost, conflict, corruption, chaos, cruelty, "and sometimes crazy."
 Advertisement Advertisement "When I talk about cruelty, I'm not just talking about treatment of immigrants," he said. "I'm talking about the treatment of Canada, of [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelensky in the White House and … the name calling, the never ending discourteous behavior," added Dent, who represented the Lehigh Valley for seven terms.
 As inflation and the war against Iran drove up the cost of petroleum this year, Trump dismissed the affordability crisis as a "Democrat hoax" and told rallygoers in Nebraska last month that the higher gas prices were a small price to pay for a non-nuclear Iran.
 Former House Majority Leader Kerry Benninghoff, a Centre County Republican who won reelection, said it was clear to those campaigning that rising prices were the primary cause of voters' frustration.
 "I hear from my daughters who do the primary amount of grocery shopping. So a lot of us knew that those were going to be some of the driving force issues, which we don't necessarily have a lot of control over."
 Advertisement Advertisement Republicans across the country need to have a deep debate over the future of the party, Dent said, adding that it will be a battle between legacy Republicans and MAGA Republicans.
 "I do think the MAGA movement is badly damaged by this," Dent said.
 SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
 Messaging and money
 Charlie Gerow, a conservative commentator and a candidate for governor in the 2022 GOP primary, said at least some of the blame falls on state Republican leaders, who he said need to get back to traditional campaigning.
 "R​​ather than having paid door knockers and a bunch of digital gobbledygook, they need real campaigns run by real people, the old-fashioned way," Gerow said.
 Advertisement Advertisement The party also failed to adequately back the top of its ticket, said Dennis Roddy, a former journalist and media strategist. He said state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, the GOP nominee for governor, was a strong candidate but wasn't able to tell her story.
 Pennsylvania Treasurer Stacy Garrity, who is seeking the GOP nomination for governor in 2026, speaks during a rally with Vice President J.D. Vance at the Uline shipping materials warehouse in Lower Macungie Township on Tuesday, Dec. 16, 2025. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)
 "If Josh Shapiro outshone Stacy Garrity, it was because he had the money to pay the electricity bill, you know, to illuminate," Roddy, who said he's no longer a member of the party, noted. "She was without funds."
 Garrity, a businesswoman and U.S. Army veteran, raised $9.2 million through mid-October compared with the $66.3 million that Shapiro's campaign spent.
 Pennsylvania Republican Party Chair Greg Rothman, a state Senator from Cumberland County, declined an interview. Spokesman James Markley said in a statement that Garrity "worked as hard, if not harder, than any candidate across the country."
 Advertisement Advertisement "As the party in power during a midterm election, Republicans around Pennsylvania and the nation put forth a full and organized effort to defy history and hold the line, but sadly that did not materialize," he said, adding that the party will analyze the results, talk with voters and prepare to come back stronger to face the challenges ahead.
 "The Republican Party of Pennsylvania remains focused on growing our movement across the Commonwealth, supporting conservative leadership, and fighting for policies that return power, freedom, and hard-earned money back to the people of Pennsylvania," Markley said.
 A clear message
 Topper, who was reelected House minority leader last week, said the first order of business is for the party "to pick a direction."
 "One of the issues that we run into now is that President Trump put together a coalition largely based on the idea of America First," he said. "I think those America First folks are confused as to what that means now with a war in the Middle East, with gas prices that they're seeing as a cause of that."
 Advertisement Advertisement Likewise, the administration's trade policies, Topper said, are unclear.
 "Are we a party of free trade? Are we a party of tariffs? Are we a party of building things in America? Are we a party of making sure that we are able to build things abroad and make things cheaper?" he asked. "Right now, we're trying to do a little bit of both, and I just don't believe that works, and I don't believe that's a clear message."
 Winning back the independent and young voters who swing elections will depend on advocating for policies that create opportunities for people of all walks of life.
 "We have to outline what the American dream is right now," Topper said, adding that homeownership, higher wages and upward mobility seem out of reach for many voters who turned to Democratic social-welfare policies for help. "That's not the American dream."
 Former U.S. Rep. Charlie Dent
 Dent, who served for 14 years in the General Assembly, agreed Pennsylvania Republicans need to have an agenda based on ideals and principles. The party for too long has focused on fealty to the president, whose goals are unclear, he said.
 Advertisement Advertisement "The party really became less of one based on ideals and principles, and more focused on following a man who has unfixed policy positions, and they shift constantly," Dent said.
 What the GOP stands for is a key question, said Gerow, suggesting that the party needs to align itself more closely with blue-collar and working-class people.
 "We have to define ourselves in those ways on the issues that matter to that constituency," he said.
 During the campaign, in which Trump implored Republicans to vote like he was on the ballot, the president appeared indifferent to the effects of his policies on regular people.
 Advertisement Advertisement Roddy, who worked as an aide to Republican ex-Gov. Tom Corbett, said the party needs to return to its past as the centrist party he joined after growing up in Cambria County in the 1960s. There, he said, Democrats were known for having a socially conservative wing.
 "The Democrats were not a progressive party. They were not a forward-thinking party. They were not a party known for tolerance and acceptance," Roddy said.
 That branch of the Democratic party was eradicated as the parties took sides on issues like abortion, guns, God and gay rights, he said.
 "But right now, the Republican Party is the one that is in most need of remediation," Roddy added, "because racism, religious bigotry, and just plain bloody mindedness have found their way into too much of the dialog."
 Looking ahead
 Dent noted that the party also suffered from a degree of complacency, noting that more than two dozen of the Republicans defeated in the U.S. House were in districts that Trump won in 2024 by 10 to 20 points. Incumbents in those districts, he said, tend to focus only on the 20% to 30% of the electorate that votes in primaries.
 Advertisement Advertisement "Well, I got news for folks: the other 70, 80% showed up, and you know you have to speak to a much broader audience," Dent said. Politics is a game played between the 40-yard lines, and for a lot of folks in both parties, this game is playing closer to the end zones, staying hard in the base."
 And while the Republican party has a deep hole to get out of in Congress and the Pennsylvania Legislature, he said it remains to be seen whether Democrats will be able to consolidate their gains.
 "Democrats need to be somewhat humble and recognize that this remarkable victory for them might be a temporary phenomenon, and that they should govern accordingly, carefully, and you know not go too far left," Dent said.
 He noted that while a wave election can take out strong incumbents, suboptimal candidates who ride the tide may prove to be vulnerable in subsequent elections.
 "It throws up a lot of driftwood on the beach, and you know there are going to be several loose logs close to the shoreline," Dent said "They're going to be pulled back in the rip tide, which will come in a cycle or two."
